Concept 02

Systems

A System is a plain Rust struct with a run method. Its meta() names every field it touches, and that declaration is the only thing the scheduler ever looks at.

In one line
A transform that declares its own reads and writes, per field, up front
You need
Nothing beyond saci-core. Concurrent stages need its default runtime feature
Read this if
You are writing your first transform, or two of your systems refuse to share a stage and you want to know which declaration is forcing them apart

What a System is

Four methods, one of them required. run receives &mut Dataset and may do anything to it. The other three are declarations about that run: what it touches, how failure is retried, and whether it needs an async state machine at all.

Rustthe trait, as declared in saci-core
#[async_trait]
pub trait System: Send + Sync {
    /// Defaults to an empty declaration named after the concrete type.
    fn meta(&self) -> SystemMeta {
        SystemMeta::new(std::any::type_name::<Self>())
    }

    /// Defaults to exponential backoff, 3 retries.
    fn config(&self) -> SystemConfig {
        SystemConfig::default()
    }

    /// The only required method.
    async fn run(&self, data: &mut Dataset) -> Result<(), SaciError>;

    /// Sync fast-path. Returning Some(_) skips the async state machine.
    fn run_sync(&self, _data: &mut Dataset) -> Option<Result<(), SaciError>> {
        None
    }
}

The executor calls run_sync first and only awaits run when it returns None, so a purely synchronous body costs no Box<dyn Future> allocation. The meta() default is an empty declaration: a system that never overrides it declares no access at all. See When meta() is wrong.

columns, and the writes that land in them the system: its declaration and its body

That system in full. Order is a component with FieldRef constants, exactly as set up on the Dataset page. The native tutorial walks a full pipeline of these from main.

Rustdeclaration and body, side by side
use std::sync::Arc;
use arrow_array::Float64Array;
use saci_core::prelude::*;

struct AddTotal;

#[async_trait]
impl System for AddTotal {
    fn meta(&self) -> SystemMeta {
        SystemMeta::new("add_total")
            .reads(Order::AMOUNT)
            .reads(Order::RATE)
            .writes(Order::TOTAL)
    }

    async fn run(&self, data: &mut Dataset) -> SaciResult<()> {
        // The view borrows `data`, so compute first, then write.
        let totals: Vec<f64> = {
            let o = data.view::<Order>()?;
            let amount = o.f64(Order::AMOUNT)?;
            let rate   = o.f64(Order::RATE)?;
            (0..o.len())
                .map(|i| amount.value(i) * rate.value(i))
                .collect()
        };

        data.apply_write_set(
            WriteSet::new().put("Order", "total", Arc::new(Float64Array::from(totals))),
        )
    }
}

apply_write_set checks that the component is registered, that the field exists in its schema, and that the array length equals the dataset's row count. It does not check the write against meta().

SystemMeta and FieldRef

SystemMeta is a name plus six lists: fields read, fields written, whole components read, whole components written, resource types read, resource types written. Every builder method takes self and returns Self, so declarations chain.

Rustthree ways to name the same access
// Typed. The component name comes from Order::name(), not a string literal.
SystemMeta::new("enrich")
    .reads(Order::AMOUNT)
    .writes(Order::TOTAL);

// Stringly. Identical effect; useful when there are no FieldRef constants.
SystemMeta::new("enrich")
    .read("Order", "amount")
    .write("Order", "total");

// Whole component. Expands to every field in the component's Arrow schema
// when the plan is built.
SystemMeta::new("ingest")
    .write_component("Order");

A FieldRef<C> is a &'static str tagged with the component type. It is zero-cost, Copy, and constructible in a const. Its only job is to stop you from pairing a field name with the wrong component, and it doubles as the argument to ComponentView accessors because it implements AsRef<str>.

Declarations are checked when the plan is built, against the dataset's SchemaRegistry. Naming an unregistered component, or a field that is not in that component's schema, is a SaciError::Configuration. The field error lists the names it did find, which is usually enough to spot the typo.

meta() is called once, when the plan is built, and the result is cached until the system set changes. A system that returns a different declaration on a later call does not get a new plan.

Why disjoint writes parallelize

Access is declared per field rather than per component, and that is what makes this work. Two systems that write different fields of the same component have no dependency on each other, so they share a stage. Two systems that write the same field are forced apart. Nothing else about the two enters the decision.

the component being written systems and the stages they land in

Systems are numbered by registration order. For any two systems i and j with i registered first, SACI adds the edge i → j when they share a field and at least one of them writes it:

  1. i writes F, j reads F: read after write.
  2. i writes F, j writes F: write after write.
  3. i reads F, j writes F: write after read.
  4. The same three cases for resources, at whole-TypeId granularity.

Two systems that only read the same field get no edge, which is why amount above is free. Edges always point from the earlier-registered system to the later one, so registration order breaks every tie and the graph cannot contain a cycle. A system's stage index is then the longest path that reaches it, and the stage list is that bucketing.

Same stage is not the same as concurrent

A stage runs its members concurrently only when every member is a ParallelSystem, there is more than one of them, and the dataset holds at least STAGE_INLINE_THRESHOLD rows, which is 100_000. A stage holding any plain System, or one under that row count, runs its members one after another on the same task, which is correct and no faster than putting them in separate stages. Sharing a stage starts to pay only once both systems are ParallelSystems and the batch is large enough.

The system_fn shortcut

For a stateless transform, such as seeding rows or printing a summary, a whole struct plus impl System is noise. system_fn pairs a SystemMeta with a closure and hands back something that implements System.

Rustmeta stays explicit; only the struct goes away
use saci_core::prelude::*;

let load = system_fn(
    SystemMeta::new("load").write_component("Order"),
    |data: &mut Dataset| {
        data.append::<Order>(&seed_rows())?;
        Ok(())
    },
);

pipeline.add_system(load);

The closure signature is Fn(&mut Dataset) -> Result<(), SaciError> + Send + Sync + 'static, synchronous by design. system_fn always implements run_sync, so these systems never build an async state machine. meta() is not optional here: the closure has no type name to fall back on, so you pass the declaration in.

Declaring resource access

Resources are the non-columnar half of a Dataset: Rust singletons keyed by TypeId. Systems declare them the same way, at coarser granularity. A resource has no fields to name, so the unit of conflict is the whole type.

Rustwhole-type granularity, not field
SystemMeta::new("convert")
    .reads(Order::AMOUNT)          // field granularity
    .writes(Order::TOTAL)
    .read_resource::<FxRates>()    // TypeId granularity
    .write_resource::<Report>();

So two systems writing the same resource type always get an edge and always land in different stages, no matter which part of it each one touches. If that ordering is costing you a stage, split the resource into two types.

A ParallelSystem only ever sees &Dataset and so cannot mutate a resource in place. Express the mutation as a ResourceUpdate attached to the returned WriteSet; the executor applies those on the main thread, after the stage's column writes have been committed.

Rustdeferred resource write from a parallel system
Ok(WriteSet::new()
    .put("Order", "score", Arc::new(Float64Array::from(scores)))
    .with_resource(ResourceUpdate::new(Report { scored: n })))

ParallelSystem and row slices

ParallelSystem is the same idea against an immutable dataset. It takes &Dataset and returns a WriteSet instead of mutating in place, which is what lets several of them run at once inside one stage. Its meta() has no default, so you must declare access.

Rustone kernel, two entry points
use std::ops::Range;

struct Score;

impl Score {
    fn compute(&self, data: &Dataset, rows: Range<u32>) -> SaciResult<Vec<f64>> {
        let o = data.view::<Order>()?;
        let amount = o.f64(Order::AMOUNT)?;
        Ok(rows.map(|i| amount.value(i as usize).log10()).collect())
    }
}

#[async_trait]
impl ParallelSystem for Score {
    fn meta(&self) -> SystemMeta {
        SystemMeta::new("score")
            .reads(Order::AMOUNT)
            .writes(Order::SCORE)
    }

    // Whole-dataset path. Always required.
    async fn run(&self, data: &Dataset) -> SaciResult<WriteSet> {
        let scores = self.compute(data, data.row_range())?;
        Ok(WriteSet::new().put("Order", "score", Arc::new(Float64Array::from(scores))))
    }

    // Opt into slice parallelism. Default returns None.
    fn run_slice(
        &self,
        data: &Dataset,
        rows: Range<u32>,
    ) -> Option<Result<SliceWriteSet, SaciError>> {
        let scores = match self.compute(data, rows.clone()) {
            Ok(s) => s,
            Err(e) => return Some(Err(e)),
        };
        Some(Ok(SliceWriteSet::new(rows).put(
            "Order",
            "score",
            Arc::new(Float64Array::from(scores)),
        )))
    }
}

pipeline.add_parallel_system(Score);

Slice parallelism is gated on two conditions, both checked before any thread is spawned. The dataset must hold at least saci_core::system::SLICE_PARALLEL_THRESHOLD rows, which is 100_000, and run_slice must return Some. When either fails, the executor calls plain run over the whole dataset instead. Below the threshold, rayon's fan-out costs more than the work it distributes.

When both hold, the row range is cut into between one and four chunks per CPU, and SACI_SLICE_CHUNKS_PER_CPU overrides the four. The chunks run under rayon inside spawn_blocking, and the results go to merge_slices. The default implementation concatenates each field's segments in slice order with arrow_select::concat::concat. Override it only when concatenation is the wrong merge, such as reducing per-slice statistics to one scalar.

Two sharp edges here. The capability check calls run_slice(data, 0..0) and throws the result away, so your implementation must tolerate an empty range without panicking. And on processor builds, where the runtime feature is off, registering a ParallelSystem is an error at run time: that path accepts plain System impls only.

When meta() is wrong

Two failure modes, and they are far apart in cost.

Naming something that does not exist is caught. When the plan is built, every declared (component, field) pair is looked up in the dataset's SchemaRegistry. An unregistered component or an unknown field is a SaciError::Configuration, and read_component / write_component fail the same way if the component is not registered. You get this from Pipeline::validate(), or from the first run, whichever comes first: both build the plan.

Declaring less than you touch is not caught. No part of the engine compares meta() against the body of run. A sequential System holds &mut Dataset and can write any registered component it likes, declared or not. An understated declaration produces missing edges, so the plan schedules dependent work as if it were independent.

The undeclared write

Two ParallelSystem impls that both write Order.total while only one declares it get no edge, share a stage, and have their write sets merged key by key. One write silently overwrites the other, and which one wins depends on task completion order. A debug_assert! catches the duplicate key in debug builds; a release build says nothing. The most common way to reach this state is to forget meta() entirely, since the default declares no access at all.

Over-declaring is the safe direction. Extra reads and writes only add edges, which costs stages and therefore wall-clock time, never correctness. If you are unsure whether a body touches a field, declare it, measure Pipeline::stage_count(), and tighten afterwards.
